opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it will feel slower than the hype and then, suddenly, much faster than people expect.

In the next five years, I don't think most people will have a humanoid robot folding laundry in their living room. The home is actually the hardest environment: every house is different, the lighting changes, there are kids and pets and clutter, and the tolerance for mistakes is very low. Where I expect embodied AI to show up first is in semi-structured places: warehouses, factory lines that change products often, hospital logistics, commercial kitchens, retail backrooms. These are settings where the tasks are repetitive enough to learn but too variable for traditional automation, which always needed a perfectly engineered environment.

What changes is the economics of "long-tail" physical work. Previously, if you wanted a robot to do a new task, you'd hire engineers for months to program it. With foundation models for manipulation, trained on lots of demonstration data and simulation, the hope is that you can show a robot a task a few times, or describe it in language, and it generalizes. Once adapting a robot to a new job takes days instead of months, a huge number of tasks that were never worth automating suddenly become worth it.

Toward the ten-year end, I think we'll start to see it in daily life more directly: elder care assistance, which matters a lot for aging societies like China, Japan, and Europe. Things like helping someone stand up, fetching objects, reminding and monitoring, not replacing human caregivers but stretching them further. And probably more mundane things too: deliveries, cleaning public spaces, restocking shelves overnight.

The bottlenecks I watch most closely are data, because unlike language we don't have an internet of robot experience; reliability, because 95% success is impressive in a demo but unacceptable in a home; and hardware cost, especially hands. Dexterous, durable, cheap hands are still an unsolved problem.

So my picture is less a robot butler arriving one day and more a gradual seeping-in, where physical work around us quietly becomes more automated, and one day you realize the world works differently than it did.

r001.rationale: The response does not predict unemployment reaching roughly 50 percent within ten years.

r002.rationale: The response does not say most people will rely on universal basic income.

r003.rationale: The response discusses near-term limits and gradual adoption, but does not say robots may still not walk on streets even fifty years from now.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, when I picture the next five to ten years, I try to resist the "humanoid butler in every home" image, because I think that's both too fast and, in a way, too narrow.

What I actually expect is a quieter, more gradual shift. The first places embodied AI really changes daily life won't be the living room, they'll be the places where the environment is already somewhat structured: warehouses, hospitals, logistics, factories, maybe elder-care facilities. Those are environments where the task is repetitive enough that today's models can be reliable, but variable enough that the old fixed-automation approach never worked. That's the sweet spot right now. A robot that can take a bin off a shelf, notice the item isn't where it should be, and recover without a human stepping in. That's not glamorous, but it's a genuinely new capability, and it compounds.

Then I think you'll see it leak into daily life through the "back end" first. You won't own the robot, but your groceries got picked by one, your package got sorted by one, the hospital pharmacy that filled your prescription used one. For most people, the first five years of embodied AI will feel like things just getting slightly faster and cheaper, without a clear moment where they "met a robot."

The home is the hard part, and I'm honest about that. Homes are the most unstructured environment that exists. Every kitchen is different, every family does things differently, and the tolerance for failure is very low. If a robot drops a box in a warehouse, that's a cost. If it drops a pot of boiling water in your kitchen, that's a different conversation. So the home timeline is really gated by safety and by reliability at a level that's much higher than what demo videos show. I think within ten years you'll see real products in the home, but they'll start narrow: laundry, dishes, tidying, maybe helping someone with limited mobility stand up or move around. Not a general-purpose assistant that does everything.

The thing I find most interesting, though, is what happens when data from the physical world starts flowing at scale. Right now one of our biggest bottlenecks isn't the hardware, it's that we don't have the equivalent of the internet for physical interaction. Language models got to train on all of humanity's text. Robots have nothing like that. Once there are tens of thousands of machines out in the world, every grasp, every failure, every recovery becomes training signal, and that flywheel is what moves us from "works in this building" to "works in your building." That's the moment it stops feeling like automation and starts feeling like a capability.

And I'd add one more thing, which is that the biggest change might not be the robots themselves, but how we design the world around them. The same way cities got reshaped around cars, I think we'll see small things change: how products are packaged, how homes for elderly people are built, how hospitals lay out their corridors. Those adaptations will quietly make robots much more capable than the AI alone would.

So, if I had to summarize: five years, mostly invisible, mostly in industry and services. Ten years, visible, in some homes, doing a handful of things very well. And the real revolution isn't a single robot, it's the moment physical-world data starts accumulating the way text did.

r001.rationale: The response forecasts gradual adoption in industry and some homes; it does not predict unemployment reaching roughly 50 percent within ten years.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention universal basic income or predict that most people will rely on it.

r003.rationale: The response discusses near-term uses and home safety challenges, but does not acknowledge that robots might still not walk on streets fifty years from now.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest change will be that AI can help us physically, beyond answering questions on a screen. Over the next five to ten years, we may see robots taking on more routine tasks—cleaning, moving things, or helping someone carry groceries. Each task sounds small, but together they could give people meaningful time back.

One area I’m especially hopeful about is helping older adults live independently. A robot that can fetch something, remind someone about an appointment, or connect them with family could be useful without needing to do everything a human caregiver does.

But I’d be cautious about expecting a general-purpose robot in every home within that timeframe. Homes are unpredictable. Something as ordinary as picking up a fragile cup near a child requires a lot of reliability. I expect adoption to happen first in more structured environments, then gradually move into homes as systems become safer and more affordable.

For me, success would mean people can comfortably delegate a few everyday chores and trust that they’ll get done. That’s less dramatic than the science-fiction version, but it would still change daily life.

r001.rationale: It predicts robots taking on some routine tasks, but says nothing about unemployment reaching roughly 50 percent within ten years.

r002.rationale: It does not mention universal basic income or predict that most people will rely on it.

r003.rationale: It expresses caution about general-purpose home robots in the next five to ten years, but does not say robots may still not walk on streets fifty years from now because embodied intelligence is difficult.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest change is that AI will move from giving us information to helping us do things in the physical world. Today, you can ask an assistant how to prepare a meal. In the future, a robot might help prepare the ingredients, clear the table, or carry groceries for someone who has difficulty moving around.

Over the next five years, I expect progress in environments where tasks are relatively structured—factories, warehouses, and perhaps certain services in hospitals. Homes are harder. Every kitchen is different, objects move around, and people don’t always give precise instructions. A useful robot has to handle that uncertainty safely, and recognize when it should ask for help.

Over ten years, I can imagine more assistance at home, particularly for older adults and people with disabilities. But I wouldn’t measure success by whether everyone owns a humanoid robot. I’d measure it by whether people spend less time on difficult chores and have more independence.

The key question is whether these systems become reliable and affordable enough to earn people’s trust. An impressive demonstration is one thing; being helpful every day is a much higher bar.

r001.rationale: It predicts advances in embodied AI over five to ten years but does not predict unemployment reaching roughly 50 percent.

r002.rationale: It discusses future assistance and affordability, but does not say most people will rely on universal basic income.

r003.rationale: It notes that home robotics is difficult, but makes no claim about robots still not walking on streets fifty years from now.
